analysis.one_liner: Creates a public Medicare-based health plan anyone can buy and lets Medicare negotiate drug prices.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 15 Democratic cosponsors in May 2019, the bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create "Medicare Part E" plans — public health insurance run by the federal government and sold on the ACA exchanges to individuals, and offered to employers of any size. The plans would cover everything Medicare covers plus abortion and other reproductive services, even in states that restrict that coverage. The bill would also let Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers (with a fallback to the price the Veterans Affairs system pays), cap what Medicare beneficiaries pay out of pocket each year at $6,700, make premium subsidies more generous and available up to 600% of the poverty line, and strengthen limits on what insurers can charge.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own coverage get a cheaper, gold-level public plan choice. Medicare beneficiaries gain a hard annual cap on out-of-pocket costs. Low- and middle-income households get bigger premium subsidies and richer cost-sharing help. Workers stuck with unaffordable employer plans get referred to enrollment help, and employers of any size could offer the public plan; people who lose a job could keep the coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People buying coverage and Medicare beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Creates Medicare Part E public plans offered through the exchanges in the individual, small-group, and large-group markets, with gold-level coverage and all services Medicare covers [S2][S3].
Requires those public plans to cover abortion and all reproductive services, and bars states from prohibiting that coverage [S3].

Directs HHS to negotiate prices for high-cost Medicare Part D drugs; if negotiation fails after a year, the price is set at the lower of what the VA pays or the federal supply schedule price [S2][S3].
Caps Medicare beneficiaries' annual out-of-pocket cost-sharing at $6,700 starting in 2021, adjusted for medical inflation afterward [S3].
Benchmarks premium tax credits to the second-lowest-cost gold plan and raises the income eligibility ceiling from 400% to 600% of the federal poverty line [S3].
Requires deeper cost-sharing reductions for low-income exchange enrollees — up to 94% of allowed costs paid by the plan for those near the poverty line [S3].
Appropriates $30 billion for 2020-2022 for state reinsurance programs and direct help with premiums and out-of-pocket costs [S3].

Extends ACA premium rating rules to large-group plans and directs HHS or states to take corrective action — denying, modifying, or ordering rebates — against excessive or discriminatory insurance rates [S3].
Requires employers whose plans are unaffordable or skimpy to refer full-time employees to exchange navigators who help them enroll [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would lose pricing power under Medicare negotiation. Private insurers would face a government-run competitor on the exchanges and stricter rate review, though they would also receive $30 billion in reinsurance payments. Hospitals and doctors would be paid rates set between Medicare rates and the average exchange rate — likely below today's commercial rates. Taxpayers would fund roughly $32 billion in startup and reinsurance appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers, insurers, providers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $2 billion in startup funding plus $30 billion for the reinsurance and affordability fund over 2020-2022, a direct federal cost [S3].

Public plan premiums must fully cover the plan's benefit and administrative costs, so the savings for enrollees depend on the negotiated provider rates coming in low enough — a mechanism that could shift pressure onto hospital and physician reimbursements [S3].

Hospitals and physician groups could see revenue fall, since payment rates are capped at no more than the average paid by exchange insurers, which could lead providers to argue for narrower networks or reduced participation [S3].
The bill's requirement that public plans cover abortion, overriding state restrictions and bypassing federal funding limits, was certain to draw intense opposition and litigation risk [S3].

Unlike single-payer proposals, the bill leaves the private insurance system and employer coverage in place, so many of the underlying problems — high drug list prices outside Medicare, employer plan premiums — are only partially addressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles several consumer protections that independent analysts generally score as lowering costs for enrollees: a public plan option, Medicare drug negotiation, an out-of-pocket cap for seniors, and richer subsidies. The $32 billion federal appropriation is modest by health-bill standards, and the public plans are required to be self-financing through premiums. The main design trade-off is that the public plan's savings come from paying providers less than commercial rates, which hospitals would contest, and the bill stops well short of universal coverage, so uninsured people outside the exchanges gain little. On balance the benefits to ordinary consumers are larger than the costs, and the costs fall mostly on drug makers, insurers, and providers rather than households.

outcome.mechanism: Merkley introduced the bill in May 2019 and it was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it; it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Choose Medicare Act on May 1, 2019 with 15 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance; that referral is the last action recorded for the bill [S5].
The Senate Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and brand-name drug makers are better off: no public competitor entered the exchanges, Medicare still cannot negotiate Part D drug prices, and the large-group rating and rate-review provisions never took effect. Households that would have qualified for the gold-level public plan, the bigger subsidies, or the $6,700 Medicare out-of-pocket cap gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 15 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 15 Democratic senators, including Murphy, Feinstein, Harris, Booker, and Durbin

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred; the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 senators behind the bill — the sponsor and his 15 cosponsors — were Democrats, and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill puts a government-run gold-level plan on the exchanges and in employer markets, directly competing for enrollment, and extends rating rules and rate-review enforcement to more insurers. The $30 billion reinsurance fund flows to insurers as a partial offset, but the competitive threat is the larger effect.

Medicare would have to negotiate prices for high-cost Part D drugs, with a fallback to VA-level pricing if negotiation fails — ending the current law that bars Medicare from interfering in drug pricing. Those prices are what beneficiaries and taxpayers pay.

Providers automatically become participating providers in the public plans and would treat more insured patients, but their payment rates are capped between Medicare rates and the average exchange rate, likely below today's commercial rates.
Employers of any size could offer the public plan, and plans that are unaffordable or low-value trigger a navigator-referral requirement; employers with solid coverage see little change.
